cards.title: A little leaks away
cards.body: Think of membrane potential as water in a beaker. Between pours, a drain removes a fraction of the water. β is the fraction KEPT, not lost.

diagram.title: Water left after each step
diagram.caption: No new input. Each step keeps 90% of the previous level.

cards.title: Keep 90%, twice
cards.body: Start at 0.5. Keep 90%: 0.5 × 0.9 = 0.45. Keep 90% again: 0.45 × 0.9 = 0.405. No input, no threshold crossing.

cards.title: Try it yourself
cards.body: Change one thing. Predict what will happen, then test it.

cards.title: Write the rule
cards.body: The symbols describe the example you just saw.

quiz.prompt: Start at 0.8, β = 0.5. What is the level after two steps with no input?
Which beaker forgets its starting water faster?
quiz.why: Keeping 60% loses 40% per step; keeping 95% loses only 5%.

retries.prompt: Start at 0.6, β = 0.5. What remains after one step?
β = 0.8. What fraction is lost each step?

misconceptions.0: β is kept. Subtract it from 1 to find the loss.

newTerms.meaning: The neuron’s changing electrical state; our water level.
A tendency for voltage to relax toward rest.
The fraction of the previous state retained per step.
Leaky integrate-and-fire: accumulate, leak, threshold, reset.

cards.title: Where the water settles
cards.body: A constant pour competes with the drain. Eventually the incoming water equals what leaks out. Here we temporarily ignore spikes and resets.

diagram.title: At equilibrium, input replaces the leak
diagram.caption: At a level of 2, a 10% leak removes exactly 0.2 per step.

cards.title: When input matches the leak
cards.body: At β = 0.9, the beaker loses 10% each step. A level of 2 loses 0.2, exactly replacing input I = 0.2.

cards.title: Write the rule
cards.body: The symbols describe the example you just saw.

quiz.prompt: With I = 0.3 and β = 0.5, what is the equilibrium without resets?
If the level is above equilibrium, what happens without resets?
quiz.why: Leak exceeds the constant input above equilibrium.

retries.prompt: I = 0.4, β = 0.8. What is the equilibrium?
Does this equilibrium formula include spike resets?
retries.why: It describes the subthreshold recurrence without resets.

newTerms.meaning: A state unchanged by another update.
The balance point between input and leak.

cards.title: The tipping line
cards.body: Add a tipping line θ. When water reaches it, the beaker tips: the neuron emits a spike, then resets. We use a hard reset to zero in this lesson.

diagram.title: The level stays below the line
diagram.caption: With β = 0.9 and I = 0.08, the no-reset equilibrium is 0.8. The spike threshold is 1.

cards.title: An input too small to trigger a spike
cards.body: With θ = 1, β = 0.9, and constant I = 0.08, the no-reset equilibrium is 0.8. Starting below threshold, this beaker never reaches 1.

cards.title: Write the rule
cards.body: The symbols describe the example you just saw.

cards.title: Can the input reach threshold?
cards.body: For v₀ below θ, β between 0 and 1, and this constant-input recurrence, I ≤ (1−β)θ cannot reach threshold in finite exact-arithmetic steps from below. Initial conditions, reset rules, and equality conventions matter.

quiz.prompt: β = 0.5, θ = 1, I = 0.4. What equilibrium would the neuron approach without resets?
Raise only the threshold under steady positive input. Usually the firing rate…
quiz.why: More accumulation is needed per spike.

retries.prompt: Start below θ = 1; β = 0.8, I = 0.1. Can constant input eventually trigger a spike?
A neuron emits 4 spikes in 20 steps. What fraction of steps had spikes?

newTerms.meaning: The state level that triggers a spike.
The state change immediately after a spike.
A discrete output event.
Spike count divided by elapsed time or steps.

cards.title: The sticky-note reference
cards.body: Delta encoding keeps a sticky note: the last SENT reconstruction, not the last reading. Emit an UP or DOWN event when the reading differs from that note by at least θ.

cards.title: The reference stays put until an event
cards.body: r = 20, θ = 1. Readings 20.3, 20.6, 20.9 produce no event. At 21.2 send UP; update r to 21, leaving a 0.2 residual. We allow one event per reading here.

cards.title: Write the rule
cards.body: The symbols describe the example you just saw.

cards.title: One event per reading
cards.body: Some encoders emit several events for a large jump until the residual is below θ. Every exercise here explicitly uses at most one event per reading.

quiz.prompt: r = 30, θ = 2. Readings: 30.8, 31.4, 32.3. After one UP event, what is r?
quiz.why: Reference moves by θ from 30 to 32; it does not become 32.3.

quiz.prompt: r = 50, θ = 1, reading = 48.7. Which event and new reference?
quiz.why: 48.7 − 50 is negative. Send DOWN and subtract exactly 1.

misconceptions.0: Read minus reference gives −1.3, so the direction is DOWN.
misconceptions.2: The note moves by one threshold, not to the raw reading.

quiz.prompt: r = 10, θ = 1. Readings 10.4, 10.8, 11.1. At which reading number is the first event?
quiz.why: Compare all three readings to the unchanged note, 10.

retries.prompt: r = 12, θ = 0.5, reading = 11.3. After one DOWN event, what is r?
r = 5, θ = 1. Readings 5.4 then 5.8. What happens?
retries.why: Neither reading is a full unit from the last sent reference.

misconceptions.1: A silent reading never updates the sticky note.

retries.prompt: r = 8, θ = 2, reading = 10.7. After one UP, what residual x − r remains?
retries.why: The new r is 10. Residual is 10.7 − 10 = 0.7.

newTerms.meaning: The reconstructed value represented by emitted events.
Encoding changes relative to a maintained reference.
A related family using accumulated quantization error; implementations vary.
The positive or negative direction of an event.
The part of the change not yet represented by events.

cards.title: One spike, many pours
cards.body: A spike travels along connections. Each connection pours its weight into a target beaker. One event can therefore cause many synaptic operations.

diagram.title: One event reaches several targets
diagram.caption: Each connection that processes a spike adds one SynOp.

items.label: One spike
items.note: An event leaves the source neuron.

cards.title: Three spikes, 128 targets each
cards.body: One spike reaching 128 target neurons triggers 128 SynOps. Three spikes with the same fan-out trigger 384.

cards.title: Write the rule
cards.body: The symbols describe the example you just saw.

quiz.prompt: 5 spikes, each with fan-out 64. How many SynOps?
A negative synaptic weight usually does what to the receiving beaker?
quiz.why: An inhibitory input pushes the membrane state downward.

retries.prompt: 2 spikes with fan-out 96: how many SynOps?
Double fan-out with the same spike count. SynOps…
retries.why: Every event touches twice as many connections.

newTerms.meaning: The strength and sign of a connection.
The number of outgoing target connections.
One event processed at one synapse.

cards.title: When sparsity pays
cards.body: Tipping rarely can reduce event processing. But counting tips alone misses the cost of updating beakers and moving state. Energy depends on the implementation.

diagram.title: Activity against an example budget
diagram.caption: Illustrative rates from one hypothetical setup; lower activity alone does not measure energy.

cards.title: Compare activity with the break-even rate
cards.body: In a hypothetical setup with break-even rate 6.4%, a rate of 8.3% is above the budget. That setup would favor its ANN baseline; these percentages are not universal constants.

cards.title: Write the rule
cards.body: The symbols describe the example you just saw.

cards.title: What the energy estimate includes
cards.body: The 6.4% break-even rate is a made-up example. A real comparison needs measured energy costs for the hardware and workload.

quiz.prompt: A measured setup breaks even at 6.4%. Its SNN runs at 8.3%. Under that setup, which is cheaper?
Which can change the energy comparison?
quiz.why: Operations, memory, and hardware all matter.

retries.prompt: A setup breaks even at 5%. Its SNN is at 3%, all other assumptions fixed. Which side is favored?
retries.why: It is below that setup’s break-even rate.

retries.prompt: 4 spikes with fan-out 50 cause how many event-driven accumulations?

newTerms.meaning: How little of a representation or activity is nonzero.
Multiply-and-accumulate operation.
Accumulate operation, often used for weighted binary events.

cards.title: A window in time
cards.body: Observe the beaker across a fixed number of steps, not just one snapshot. Events form a sequence across that window.

diagram.title: Three events in ten steps
diagram.caption: Each vertical mark is a spike; empty steps still count toward the window.

cards.title: Count spikes over a whole window
cards.body: A 10% spike fraction over 30 steps means 3 spikes for a neuron. A time step is a simulation increment; it is not automatically one millisecond.

cards.title: Write the rule
cards.body: The symbols describe the example you just saw.

quiz.prompt: A neuron spikes in 20% of 40 steps. How many spikes?
Can you convert 30 simulation steps into seconds without knowing step duration?
quiz.why: You need Δt to convert steps to physical time.

retries.prompt: 3 spikes in 60 steps. What is the spike fraction?
A window has 50 steps of 2 ms each. Duration in ms?

newTerms.meaning: One discrete increment in a simulation.
The number of steps over which activity is measured.

cards.title: Why spikes resist gradients
cards.body: The tip indicator is a switch. A tiny change below the line usually does not change the output. At the line, it jumps abruptly.

diagram.title: The hard spike is a switch
diagram.caption: Output stays 0 below threshold and jumps to 1 at θ. A small change on either flat side gives no slope.

cards.title: A small voltage change, the same output
cards.body: With θ = 1, both 0.8 and 0.81 output 0. At threshold the output jumps to 1. There is no useful ordinary slope for gradient learning.

cards.title: Write the rule
cards.body: The symbols describe the example you just saw.

quiz.prompt: Away from threshold, the ordinary derivative of the hard spike function is…
quiz.why: On either flat side a small voltage change leaves the binary output unchanged.

quiz.prompt: At the jump, its ordinary derivative is…
quiz.why: A discontinuity has no ordinary derivative there.

retries.prompt: Move voltage from 0.3 to 0.31 with θ = 1. The hard spike output…
Why is the exact hard-spike derivative unhelpful for backpropagation?
retries.why: Zero gradients prevent ordinary updates through the spike decision.

options.text: It is zero away from the jump
It is too expensive to store

newTerms.meaning: A point where an ordinary derivative does not exist.
A step function used to model a binary spike decision.

cards.title: A useful pretend slope
cards.body: Keep the real tipping switch when running the neuron. During backward learning, replace its unusable slope with a smooth proxy near the line.

diagram.title: A slope for the backward pass
diagram.caption: Sampled backward slope for k = 1. The proxy peaks near threshold; the forward spike stays binary.

cards.title: Hard spikes forward, a proxy slope backward
cards.body: A hard decision still outputs 0 or 1. A chosen proxy might give backward slope 1 at threshold and 0.25 one scaled unit away.

cards.title: Write the rule
cards.body: The symbols describe the example you just saw.

quiz.prompt: A surrogate gradient changes which part?
quiz.why: The forward spike can remain hard and binary.

options.text: Every forward spike into a probability

quiz.prompt: For k = 1 and |v−θ| = 1, what is this proxy slope?

retries.prompt: Does a nonzero surrogate slope prove the forward neuron spiked?
retries.why: The proxy is for learning, not a record of an event.

retries.prompt: k = 1, |v−θ| = 0. What is the proxy slope?

newTerms.meaning: A proxy derivative used for a hard spike function.
A backward approximation through a discrete operation.
A commonly used proxy with a concentrated slope near threshold.
